**How does your proposal relate to HSEE?** It empowers humans collectively and biologically. Collectively, it gives small organizations a low-cost legal mechanism to steer military-industrial lobbying toward cure-finding instead of arms-race maintenance. Biologically, the 1% Treaty funds pragmatic clinical trials at scale, increasing the evidence base for healthspan, cognition, and disease treatment. Humans cannot keep pace with AI while preventable disease keeps deleting their time, attention, and coordination capacity.

**12-month HSEE milestones:** Within 12 months, we expect to complete securities counsel review, publish the shareholder-demand package, build the first public survey/registry workflow, contact at least 1,000 nonprofits, secure 100-200 campaign endorsements if conversion rates match the landmine/ICAN-style outreach model, and deliver the first donated-share demand letters to military-contractor boards.

**Past HSEE-related projects:** Mike built the open-source precursor to the decentralized FDA at studies.dfda.earth, collecting about 12 million data points from over 10,000 people and applying causal inference to quantify effects of foods, drugs, and behaviors on health conditions. The current dFDA and 1% Treaty work generalize that patient-centered evidence system to pragmatic trials, healthspan, and AI-assisted collective coordination.

**Equitable distribution:** The treaty design targets universal access by funding pragmatic trials through public, auditable allocation rather than donor-controlled steering. The survey/registry asks people which diseases and outcomes should receive priority, and the allocation system is designed so capital buys no governance control. The point is not premium enhancement for a small class. It is a larger evidence engine for treatments that can reach everyone.

## B. Theory of change

### B1. The mechanism

> "The military-industrial complex is not a sovereign power. It is a collection of publicly traded corporations whose shares are for sale to anyone with a brokerage account. The lobby that has driven military budget expansion for eighty years is a line item in those corporations' SG&A. The line item is controllable by whoever holds the board. The board is electable by whoever holds 50%+1 of the shares. The shares are for sale." (loving-takeover.qmd)

**The donation-funded campaign (this grant):** a campaign coordinator replicates the playbook that banned landmines and nuclear weapons. The International Campaign to Ban Landmines started in 1992 with six NGOs; Jody Williams grew it to 1,400 organizations in 90 countries in five years using email and a fax machine, 122 countries signed, and she won the Nobel Peace Prize; ICAN repeated it for nuclear weapons with five staff in Geneva. This campaign adds one upgrade. Instead of asking each nonprofit for an endorsement (cheap talk), the coordinator **donates one share of a military contractor to each endorsing nonprofit**, which then, as a shareholder of record, sends the board a pre-drafted shareholder demand, equal parts love letter and Caremark notice:

- *The love:* we do not want you and everyone you love to be slowly tortured and murdered by horrible diseases, and you are on the same actuarial table as everyone else.
- *The fiduciary case:* board members owe shareholders their best financial judgment, and the numbers favor pivoting. Biotech margins beat cost-plus munitions margins. The treaty world's economy is modeled at {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_15 >}} the size of the current trajectory at year 15 (gdp-trajectories.qmd), and the {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}}/year trial market is a new revenue line these companies are better positioned than anyone to capture. Meanwhile their flagship product line holds inventory for {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} apocalypses in a market that supports one.
- *The ask:* divest weapons lines with negative externalities exceeding revenue (autonomous weapons first), reinvest in biotechnology, and redirect the lobbying budget toward the 1% Treaty. Same lobbyists, same senators, same lunches. The machine just starts asking for medicine money.

A board is legally obliged to read a shareholder demand. One letter from one activist is filed; hundreds of separate demands from named nonprofits (each with its own members and press list) are a campaign the board must answer. The share is also a commitment device: an organization that accepts property and takes a legal action is bound to the campaign in a way no petition signature achieves. Cost per nonprofit: one share (~$150–600) plus a letter template drafted once and reused hundreds of times. (Legal note, stated honestly: a single share confers demand-letter standing and annual-meeting attendance; formal Rule 14a-8 shareholder proposals require ~$25k held one year, which becomes the year-2 escalation for organizations that hold.)

**The escalation path (funded by investment, not this grant):** if letters don't persuade, shares do. Engine No. 1 won three ExxonMobil board seats in 2021 holding 0.02% of shares, on a platform of accelerating the energy transition; the stock went up. Three institutional investors hold 60-75% of every major military contractor, and their mandate is share value, so the pitch to them is the same fiduciary case in the letter. Each tier of ownership is insurance against the cheaper tier failing; capital climbs only as far as persuasion fails. Full cost of certainty (50.1% of everything, needing nobody's agreement): {{< var defense_takeover_cost_total >}}, or ~{{< var defense_takeover_cost_per_human >}} per global human. Nobody needs that on day one.

### B1a. Coalition scale and leverage

There is no knowable number of organizations "required" to pass a treaty. The defensible benchmark is the observed scale of civil-society coalitions that already did it. The International Campaign to Ban Landmines grew from six NGOs to over 1,000 organizations and 122 state signatures [@icbl-ottawa-treaty]. ICAN now lists about 650 partner organizations across 110 countries, and the nuclear-ban treaty was adopted by 122 states [@ican-nuclear-ban-treaty]. The cluster-munitions process moved from 46 states signing the Oslo Declaration to 94 states signing the convention, again with close civil-society participation [@cluster-munitions-convention-2008].

This campaign uses that history as an engineering target, not a guarantee. The base request funds the first share-backed wave: up to ~300 organizations with actual shareholder standing, plus the legal package and outreach system. The ambitious $850,000 request funds share capacity at the landmine-campaign order of magnitude: up to 1,400 one-share transfers at a $350 blended price (~$490,000), plus one coordinator ($150,000), the demand-letter/legal package ($40,000), registry infrastructure ($30,000), securities/compliance review ($50,000), and contingency (~$90,000).

The political ask is milder than the precedents. Landmines, cluster munitions, and nuclear weapons campaigns asked states to ban whole weapons classes. This asks states to redirect 1% of military spending simultaneously, so relative military power is unchanged, while the redirected money creates a legally bound health-research funding stream. The shareholder demand also has legal force before the treaty exists: boards must process demands from shareholders, and a nonprofit that accepts a share and sends the letter has done more than endorse. It has become part of the legal record.

The grant's funding leverage is the main point. The base request is $400,000. The treaty redirects {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}}/year, with {{< var dih_treasury_trial_subsidies_annual >}}/year reaching direct pragmatic-trial subsidies after allocations and platform costs. That is about 68,000 dollars redirected per grant dollar in the first treaty year, or about 54,000 direct trial-subsidy dollars per grant dollar. The probability threshold is therefore very low: if this grant has more than a ~0.0015% chance of being pivotal for even one year of treaty funding, it is positive in redirected dollars before counting the health value, GDP effects, peace dividend, or recurring treaty years. The $1B Incentive Alignment Bond campaign remains the conservative full-campaign baseline; the share-backed coalition is the cheaper path being tested here.

Do not describe this as a personal financial return on the grant. For SFF, it is philanthropic leverage:

| Frame for SFF | If this $400,000 grant is pivotal | At 1% pivotal probability |
|---|---:|---:|
| First-year gross treaty funding | 68,000x | 680x expected |
| First-year direct trial subsidies | 54,000x | 540x expected |
| 20-year gross treaty funding, no discounting | 1,360,000x | 13,600x expected |
| 20-year direct trial subsidies, no discounting | 1,085,000x | 10,850x expected |

### B2. What the treaty buys (the arithmetic, walked through)

The full derivation is public, parameterized, and Monte Carlo'd (health-dividend.qmd, 1-pct-treaty-impact.qmd); the napkin version:

1. **Funding:** 1% of global military spending = {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}}/year. After investor and political-incentive allocations ({{< var dih_treasury_medical_research_pct >}} reaches medical research) and operating costs, {{< var dih_treasury_trial_subsidies_annual >}}/year remains for trial subsidies.
2. **Price per patient:** traditional Phase 3 trials cost {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}/patient. Embedded pragmatic trials cost {{< var dfda_pragmatic_trial_cost_per_patient >}} (ADAPTABLE basis; Oxford's RECOVERY achieved {{< var recovery_trial_cost_per_patient >}}; a systematic review of 64 embedded pragmatic trials found a median of {{< var pmc_pragmatic_trial_median_cost_per_patient >}}).
3. **Capacity:** {{< var dih_treasury_trial_subsidies_annual >}} ÷ {{< var dfda_pragmatic_trial_cost_per_patient >}} = {{< var dih_patients_fundable_annually >}}, versus {{< var current_trial_slots_available >}} enrolled globally today = **{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}}** trial capacity.
4. **Timeline:** {{< var diseases_without_effective_treatment >}} have zero approved treatments; at the current rate of {{< var new_disease_first_treatments_per_year >}}, clearing the backlog takes {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}}. At {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}} capacity: {{< var dfda_queue_clearance_years >}}. The average untreated disease gets its first treatment {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_treatment_acceleration_years >}} earlier.
5. **Plus the efficacy lag:** drugs that have passed safety testing wait another {{< var efficacy_lag_years >}} for efficacy confirmation while patients who could take them die. Combined timeline shift: {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_years >}}.
6. **Stakes:** the combined shift is modeled at {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_dalys >}} of healthy life (paste the full 95% CI; the parameter is marked low-confidence in our own documentation, and the conclusion below survives the bottom of the interval).

### B3. Cost-effectiveness, with the skeptic's discounts already applied

- **Conditional on success:** {{< var treaty_cost_per_daly_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}} per DALY, versus {{< var bed_nets_cost_per_daly >}}/DALY for bed nets (GiveWell's gold standard). That is {{< var treaty_vs_bed_nets_multiplier >}} more cost-effective, at vastly greater scale.
- **Risk-adjusted:** at the modeled political success probability ({{< var political_success_probability >}}), expected cost per DALY is {{< var treaty_expected_cost_per_daly >}}, still {{< var treaty_expected_vs_bed_nets_multiplier >}} better than bed nets.
- **If the treaty never passes:** direct philanthropic funding of pragmatic trials alone achieves {{< var dfda_direct_funding_cost_per_daly >}}/DALY, competitive with GiveWell's top interventions. The trial model does not depend on the politics; the politics multiply it.
- **The pessimist's version:** take this grant in isolation and assign the campaign whatever success probability you like. At 0.1%, a $37,000 coordinator-plus-shares budget against $27.2B/year of redirected trial funding averting DALYs at $929/patient works out to roughly $1.23 per expected DALY. At 0.001% (one in a hundred thousand) it is still ~$123/DALY, competitive with the best direct interventions in the world. The question is not whether the campaign probably succeeds; it is whether its probability of success is really below one in a hundred thousand.

> "This costs less per life-year than mosquito nets and nobody has heard of it." (health-dividend.qmd)

### B4. Why this is an x-risk intervention

Two links to AI risk, one concrete and one structural:

- **Concrete:** board control can wind down autonomous-weapons programs at the source (not lobbied against, but cancelled by the owners voting). These are programs whose externalities exceed their revenue; divesting them is consistent with, not contrary to, fiduciary duty.
- **Structural:** government budgets are the largest revealed-preference dataset any AI will train on, and the current one says killing matters {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio_nounit >}} times more than testing cures. As the book puts it: *"Your AI isn't misaligned. It's a mirror... A misaligned AI might build hospitals. Yours won't. It's a very good student."* (moronia.qmd) Flip the allocation and the mirror has something better to copy.

**Capture safeguard (one paragraph, because SFF asks about power concentration):** redirected treaty funds flow through an auditable, open-source, forkable allocation system in which capital buys no steering: one human, one voice, with 80% of funds structurally untouchable by any donor, board, or investor, and outcome measurement computed from five independent data sources so no single institution can quietly game it. Money buys returns; it never buys influence. Details: [optimocracy](https://manual.warondisease.org/knowledge/appendix/optimocracy-paper.html) [@optimocracy-paper-2025].qmd, [wishocracy](../solution/wishocracy.qmd) [@wishocracy-paper-2025].qmd, theory-of-operation.qmd.

The plan also includes an accountability venue ([Court of Humanity](../solution/court-of-humanity.qmd) [@court-of-humanity-paper-2025], with the treaty as its standing settlement offer), a global referendum, and an AI-tutored education layer, all documented in the book (court-of-humanity.qmd, global-referendum.qmd, special-education.qmd). This application funds only the shareholder campaign and its supporting infrastructure.

## C. What we would do with the funding (use of funds)

The grant funds a campaign coordinator running the ICBL/ICAN playbook with shareholder teeth:

- **Campaign coordinator, 24 months** (~$6,200/month). Contacts 8–10 nonprofits per day, explains the treaty, and makes each endorsing organization a concrete offer: accept one donated share of a military contractor, send the pre-drafted shareholder demand to its board, and email your members the two-question global survey (how should trial resources be allocated across diseases; would you support a 1% reallocation from military spending to clinical trials). Six-month benchmark from the ICBL rate: 1,000–1,300 organizations contacted, 100–200 endorsements. **$150,000** (24 months at ~$6,200/month).
- **The shares.** One share per endorsing nonprofit, assigned across the big military contractors so every major board receives demands from many separate shareholders. **$105,000** (~300 shares at a ~$350 blended price).
- **The demand letter + fiduciary evidence package.** Drafted once with securities counsel, served hundreds of times: the Caremark notice, the love letter, the GDP-trajectory model, the biotech-margin comparison, and the per-company pivot analysis. All parameterized, all public. **$40,000**.
- **Survey + signer registry infrastructure** (open-source). **$30,000**.
- **Legal/compliance.** Securities counsel for the share-gifting mechanics and antitrust/CFIUS review before any organized share program scales. **$50,000**.

Total: **$375,000** over 24 months; requested at **$400,000** with a ~7% contingency.

**Ambitious coalition-scale budget:** **$850,000**. This replaces the $105,000 share line with up to **$490,000** for 1,400 one-share transfers at a $350 blended price, preserving the coordinator, demand-letter, registry, and legal/compliance lines above, with roughly $90,000 contingency for price movement, legal review, and faster-than-expected conversion. This is the version that can honestly say it bought share capacity at the scale of the successful landmine coalition.

Every dollar maps to a countable output: organizations contacted, endorsements, shares transferred, demands served, survey responses.

## D. Track record / evidence we can execute

The complete plan is written, parameterized, and public: a book-length manual ("How to End War and Disease") where every number links to its own derivation, data source, and 95% confidence interval (warondisease.org).

Each mechanism has already worked at least once:

- **Cheap pragmatic trials:** Oxford's RECOVERY trial spent {{< var recovery_trial_cost_per_patient >}}/patient (traditional: {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}), tested treatments on ~48,000 patients during a pandemic, and saved over 1 million lives, an {{< var recovery_trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} efficiency gain. (recovery-trial.qmd)
- **Board control without majority ownership:** in 2021, twelve-person hedge fund Engine No. 1 won three ExxonMobil board seats holding 0.02% of shares, on a platform of accelerating the energy transition. The stock went up. (loving-takeover.qmd)
- **War-to-research reallocation producing a medical golden age:** after WWII the US cut real military spending ~94% (over $800B to $48B constant dollars by 1948) while NIH funding went from under $3 million to $50 million by 1950, then grew another 500% through the 1950s. The results of that window: the Salk polio vaccine (1955, deaths down 50% in one year), the structure of DNA (1953), the Framingham Heart Study (1948). The most productive era of medical progress in history happened because resources moved from war to research. The treaty proposes the same reallocation at 1% of the scale. **[VERIFY: NIH figures against references.bib before submitting]**
- **Paid peace:** Egypt and Israel fought four wars in twenty-five years; since 1979 the US has paid both governments a few billion dollars a year, and there have been zero wars in the forty-six years since. (department-of-peace.qmd)
- **Small coalitions passing weapons treaties:** the International Campaign to Ban Landmines went from six NGOs (1992) to 1,400 organizations in 90 countries in five years, using email and a fax machine; 122 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty and Jody Williams won the Nobel Peace Prize. ICAN repeated the playbook for nuclear weapons with five staff: 600+ organizations, 122 states voting yes, another Nobel. Chemical weapons (1993, 193 countries) and biological weapons (1975, 187 countries) fell to the same pattern. Those campaigns asked nations to give up weapons entirely; this treaty asks them to buy 1% fewer.

**Founder track record (Mike P. Sinn):**

- Built and shipped the open-source precursor to the decentralized FDA: a platform ([studies.dfda.earth](https://studies.dfda.earth)) that collected ~12 million data points from over 10,000 people and applied causal inference to quantify the effects of thousands of foods and drugs on dozens of health conditions. The dFDA protocol in this application is that system generalized, not a paper design.
- Wrote "How to End War and Disease" over several years and maintains a public [papers and publications index](../papers.qmd) with 24 entries, including the treaty impact model, dFDA specification and impact, [Incentive Alignment Bonds](../solution/incentive-alignment-bonds.qmd) [@iab-paper-2025], Optimal Policy/Budget Generators, and [GDP trajectories](../economics/gdp-trajectories.qmd) [@gdp-trajectories-paper-2025].
- Foresight Institute Fellow.
- Background: electrical engineering; invented a power-line modem; 10 years operating and then managing an industrial testing laboratory, performing root-cause failure analysis and building laboratory information management systems. That is a career spent finding out why complex systems fail and building the data infrastructure that proves it, which is this project at civilizational scale: root-cause analysis of why cures don't get found, and the information management system for the trials that find them.

Current campaign traction: no referendum signatures or endorsing organizations are claimed in this application yet; this grant funds the first formal outreach wave. Shipped assets include the public manual, the public [papers and publications index](../papers.qmd), the parameter engine, the studies.dfda.earth precursor platform, and draft shareholder-demand / coalition infrastructure.

## E. The returnable instrument: EOS equity (for Funders who prefer an investment / matching pledge)

Separate from the grant. Earth Optimization Services Inc. is a Berkshire-model holding company that buys activist positions in military contractors and uses shareholder power to (a) pivot their assets toward biotechnology, and (b) redirect their {{< var defense_lobbying_annual >}}/year lobbying toward the 1% Treaty, which creates the {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}}/year trial-subsidy market those same companies can then sell into.

- **Shares are non-voting.** "Your money buys a return, not a vote, because EOS's mission is locked. EOS's money buys votes, in other people's boardrooms, which is the entire product." (earth-optimization-services.qmd)
- **The downside, in full (verbatim):** "If none of it works: your money is not gone. It is sitting in shares of real companies. EOS liquidates the portfolio, distributes to equity holders. You get back whatever military-contractor and pharma stocks returned over the holding period. No carry, no management fee. The floor is 'you accidentally bought a military-contractor ETF with no fees.'"
- **The upside is projected, never guaranteed:** modeled appreciation as the treaty enlarges the economy the portfolio sits in and the biotech pivot opens higher-margin product lines. You are buying sole-supplier monopolies whose customer cannot leave, and redirecting their discretionary spending toward higher-return opportunities.
- **Convergence:** an investor who cares only about returns and an investor who cares only about canceling autonomous-weapons programs take the identical action. The campaign requires no shared motivation, only shared action.

*(Securities note: all upside figures are projected/modeled; binding terms live in the PPM, not this application. Accredited investors only.)*

## H. HSEE Theme Supplemental

**How this enhances/empowers humans to keep pace with AI:**

**1. Biomedical capability floor.** The bottleneck on human enhancement (cognitive, longevity, and otherwise) is not ideas but trial capacity: {{< var diseases_without_effective_treatment >}} have zero approved treatments, {{< var new_disease_first_treatments_per_year >}} get their first treatment per year, and drugs proven safe wait {{< var efficacy_lag_years >}} more to reach patients. The decentralized-FDA protocol multiplies trial capacity {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}} and collapses that lag. Fixing the discovery engine is the precondition for any biological self-enhancement agenda: humans cannot keep pace with AI while losing decades of healthy life to untreated disease.

**2. Cognitive/coordination augmentation.** Free, AI-tutored education that teaches every human the plan to exactly the level their role needs, paired with AI agents that let one person coordinate at population scale. Humans evolved to coordinate hunting parties of ~20 and max out around 150 relationships (Dunbar's number); the job now requires coordinating billions. Closing that gap is the enhancement. (special-education.qmd, ai-coordination-army.qmd)

**The framing SFF asks for** ("how current treatment of humans shapes future AI values") inverts cleanly: a civilization whose budget funds weapons {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio_nounit >}} times more than cure-testing is publishing that ratio as its revealed preference, the training signal every AI built inside it reads. *"A misaligned AI might build hospitals. Yours won't. It's a very good student."* (moronia.qmd) Change the curriculum and you change what it learns to value.

## Closing (use as the final free-text answer or cover note)

We think this is the most cost-effective way to avert disability-adjusted life years per dollar that anyone has proposed. That is a strong claim, so we ask two things:

1. If you see a factual or logical error in the analysis above, tell us. Every parameter, formula, and confidence interval is public and clickable, and we will correct the model and republish.
2. If you know of an intervention that averts a DALY at a lower expected cost, please send us the analysis, and we will redirect our own effort to that instead.
